title: How Much Fun Can One Button Create? | One-Button Game Design

scenes.title: One button, many decisions
lines: If a game has only one button, can it only do one thing?
Kirby's minigames, Canabalt, and Geometry Dash suggest otherwise. The same button can lead to very different decisions.
Your finger uses the same button, but the decisions in your head are completely different.
Let's explore four approaches to one-button play, and how a small set of controls can still create interesting games.

scenes.title: Mashing: how fast can you press?
lines: The first approach is button mashing: competing to press as quickly as possible within a limited time.
The explanation is simple. Each press adds power, and faster presses take you farther. The screen can communicate the rule before anyone explains it.
But repeating the same movement for a long time can be tiring, and people differ in how quickly they can press.
So, rather than demanding endless repetition, short bursts of effort separated by rest may be a better fit.
Mashing is not inherently bad. It is an input whose effort and momentary tension need a purpose.

scenes.title: Timing: will pressing now hit the target?
lines: The second approach is timing. Kirby's Megaton Punch asks you to align power, position, and the final moment. In Geometry Dash, you read approaching obstacles and choose when to jump.
More presses do not mean better play. What matters is reading the motion and waiting for the right moment.
With the same button, a wider target can create a forgiving activity, while a narrower target can create a precision challenge.
It also helps to show whether a failed press was slightly early or slightly late. That tells the player what to change next time.
If they think, 'Ah, I should have waited one more beat,' they are already preparing for another attempt.

scenes.title: Reaction: press when the signal appears
lines: The third approach is reaction. In Samurai Kirby, you try to press faster than your opponent after a signal appears.
Timing games often ask you to anticipate a moment. Reaction games focus more on recognizing that the signal has actually appeared.
You want to press quickly, but pressing too early means failure. Even a wait in which nothing happens can become tense.
Making the signal hard to perceive is not the same as making the wait exciting.
Use multiple cues rather than relying only on color or sound, and make the criteria for success and failure clear.

scenes.title: Holding and releasing: what should you accept?
lines: The fourth approach is switching between holding the button and releasing it.
In Kirby's Egg Catcher, you hold for eggs and release for bombs. Things approach from the same direction, but you must decide what to accept and what to avoid.
This is not a toggle that switches a function on or off with each press. What matters is whether the button is being held right now.
The player reads the approaching object and decides whether to maintain or change their action.
You have not hidden lots of functions behind one button. Two states can already produce different choices in different situations.

scenes.title: Simple input, clear results
lines: Now let's put the same button on two screens. On the left, only a number changes. On the right, the button moves down, an object jumps, and the result is easy to read.
Even with identical rules, the experience can change depending on how clearly the game communicates your input and its consequence.
Canabalt also runs with a single jump button. Both when you press and how long you hold affect the jump, so you must adapt to the gaps and obstacles ahead.
Holding can serve as a confirmation that prevents mistakes, or as a way to choose jump height or when to launch.
But more screen shake and louder sound do not automatically make better feedback. First, make the information needed for the next decision clear.

scenes.title: Design the decision before the button
lines: In short: mashing focuses on speed, timing on a moment, reaction on a signal, and holding or releasing on a state.
When designing controls, start with what the player observes and when they decide, rather than how many buttons you need.
Then check whether the result is immediately understandable and whether the player can see why an attempt failed.
One button can be enough. If the reason to press it is interesting, the game has already begun.
